content.summary_of_the_paper: This work focuses on the problem of Nash equilibrium (NE) finding in a class of continuous general-sum N-player games where the payoff is a composite of convex function and quadratic operator. The work identifies a set of sufficient conditions for global NE by leveraging canonical duality theory and variational inequalities and proposes a continuous-time learning dynamics as well as a discretized algorithm that probably converges. Numerical experiments show that the proposed method manages to converge to the global NE.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

- This work makes contribution towards computing global NE in non-convex games, which has been an important yet challenging topic. 
- Numerical experiments verify that the proposed method converges to the global NE, while typical gradient-based methods typically converge to a Nash stationary point.

Weaknesses:

- Some theoretical results need further clarification. In particular, Theorem 2 shows that the converging point of the proposed continuous-time learning dynamics is a global NE when it meets certain gradient condition, which is missing in Theorem 3. Please clarify if the converging point $z^{\mathbin{\Diamond}}$ in Theorem 3 is indeed a global NE. (similar comment on Theorem 4 and 5).

- The discretized method is studied in two typical scenarios: monotone games and potential games. It would be great if the authors can comment on the technical challenges of presenting a more general result (i.e., in the setting of Theorem 3). In addition, a discussion on the comparison of convergence rate with prior results would be helpful.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: See "Strength and weaknesses". The work appears to be novel and original.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper offers an interesting study of N-player nonconvex games in which the individual utility functions satisfy certain assumptions that are quite common in the literature of machine learning and, as such, the topic of the study is well justified. The solution concept adopted by the authors is that of the (global) Nash equilibrium (GNE) which is contrasted to Nash stationary points. The latter is a superset of the GNE and are deemed as less desirable. In order to compute/calculate such points, the authors use canonical duality theory to come up with a ODE system whose equilibria are a superset of the GNE's. The authors reach to the formulation of this ODE by first making the following observations:
i) a Nash stationary point is a stationary point for each player's complementary function
ii) the stationary points of the complementary functions are cast as a variational inequality problem
iii) generating functions are used to couple primal and dual variables together and in turn, a gradient flow dynamic is applied upon the variational inequality problem
The authors prove that the ODE converges and under some conditions, the point of convergence is a (global) Nash equilibrium. Additionally, the latter ODE is discretized in order to be implementable and some additional convergence theorems are provided.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:

        "Moreover, with the interference of xâˆ’i, the problem reflects a cluster of Î“i with a mutual coupling of stationary conditions, rather a deterministic one."

Questions/Remarks:
    * The authors have not examined whether or not a (global) Nash equilibrium exists in the settings they are studying. Their existence is nontrivial.
    * Since the algorithm assumes communication between the players, why does the Nash equilibrium remain the solution concept of choice?

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper focuses on the problem of finding equilibria for a class of non-convex games where each player's loss/utility function is a composition of two (nested) functions of the full vector of all players' actions: 
1. The first function of the composition is a vector-valued map (potentially nonconvex), which importantly, needs to satisfy that *the second derivative does not contain (part of) the optimization variable*.
2. The outer real-valued function needs to be a convex differential canonical function.

One can see that the former is quite a restrictive assumption, but it yet includes some problems that are not included in the monotone VIs class of problems.

The approach of the paper is to:
1. use canonical conjugate transformation, a technique from the so-called *canonical duality theory* described in [Gao et al, 2017]
2. the stationary conditions of the transformed problem then yield  a VI
3. the VI is solved via an ODE in the dual space
4. the mapping back in the primal space is done through conjugate gradients

To obtain a practical algorithm, the ODE is discretized.
Convergence guarantees are also provided in both continuous and discrete times.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths.**
- The paper considers a highly relevant problem. 
- Combines interesting ideas from duality.
- The presented results are technically non-trrivial and very interesting from theoretical perspective.

**Weaknesses.**
- The considered problem is yet a restrictive problem class, and there is no discussion if this approach may be extended or not.
- The writing and structure can be significantly improved (see the section  below)
- Missing related works discussions and comparisons (see below)
- The simulations in Fig. 4 lack comparison with the common VI methods such as extragradient, proximal point, optimistic gradient, etc.; there is no wall-clock time comparison for different dimensions etc.


## Missing Related Works discussions
Related works are somewhat ignored in this work, what needs to be fixed. A discussion on known lower bounds for some broader problem class, known rates, etc would be helpful, as well as contrasting the setup, the rates etc with previous ones. Most surprisingly, the authors do not discuss how the approach herein differs from existing methods for some non-convex problem classes.
Also:
- The end of 4th paragraph is very unclear: the authors seem to mention some highly relevant works to this one (as these also focus on non-convex cases), yet they do not explain how these differ, or motivate which particular drawback these methods have that will be solved in this paper.



### Minor
- Abstract: it is very unclear which class of nonconvex N-player games this work focuses on; please be specific in the abstract 
- Sec 1, 1st paragraph: I don't understand why strongly-concave cases are listed as non-convex games?
- Sec 1, 2nd paragraph: I gues in last sentence you mean "generative adversarial training" and not "adversarial learning"?
- Sec 1, 3rd par.: be precise that you mean convexity assumptions on the players' payoff/loss.
- Sec 1, 4th par.: may be more suitable to use methods instead of processes
- Sec 1: motivate your choices that are just listed in the last par.; this section is intended to explain why you approach this problem in such a way; also, it is very hard to follow, hence, use bullet points for example and describe better
- The correct citation for GANs is Goodfellow et al. 2014
- Provide definition for convex differential canonical function
- Consider moving the  setup description from Sec. 2 in Sec. 1 as well as describing the setup in the abstract; as otherwise the reader needs to guess what "canonical functions and quadratic operators" means are up until Sec. 2, and it is very unclear up to that point.
- Similarly, move the definition of convex differentiable canonical function where the setup is defined, or at least point to its definition in Sec. 3 where it is mentioned in Sec. 2 (otherwise seems like the reader needs to find it in the cited book in order to proceed reading).
- when citing books for some specific context, list the section number as well
- do you mean conex *diferentiable* canonical functions? 
- I am not sure I understand the purpose of Fig. 3, wouldn't such trend appear even i
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Writing / Clarity**.
I found this paper relatively hard to follow, for example:
- The introduction focuses a lot on motivating general non-convex games, which is relatively clear; and yet only rushes through the motivation for this specific setup (also presents no motivation for the specific approach taken here, nor introduce/summarize the advantages of canonical conjugate transformation).
- Some definitions relevant to follow the introduction are given later (e.g. in Sec. 2 or 3) making it hard to follow it.
- Some assumptions are not explicitly stated as assumptions (such as the assumption on the second-order derivative of the payoff functions), and the theorems do not state the assumptions.


**Reproducibility.**
I did not find any details on the implementation. Please include such a section in the appendix.


## Questions
1. To understand better the problem class, could you provide some examples where the jacobian of the joint vector field (the second-order derivatives for the N players) does not have a dependence on the variable in the diagonal terms but has such dependence on the off-diagonal terms? 
2. Is the assumption that the second-order derivatives are $x$-free only used for the $\epsilon_i^+$ set? Do you think it is possible to generalize this setup and remove/relax that assumption?
3. What are the assumptions that need to hold, so that $\epsilon_i^+$  is easy to compute? Also, what is the added complexity in the most general case?
4. Could you comment on the conjugate gradient and the assumption that the payoffs have these assumed quadratic terms? more precisely, how can you 
5. What is the lower bound for this problem class, and does your convergence rate match it?
6. What is the y-axis in Fig. 4?  Also, could you provide the corresponding plots where the x-axis is wall clock time?
7. Could you provide comparisons with the proximal point method? 
8. Could you provide a wall-clock time comparison with standard VI methods on monotone VIs for example?
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper focuses on an interesting class of problems that may help advance the optimization of N-player games, that is general non-monotone VIs. It combines interesting insights from duality and derives an algorithm designed to converge solely to a global equilibrium, and provides convergence guarantees.  

Several aspects could be significantly improved, such as writing and presentation, lack of related works and comparisons, adding missing discussions on the limitations, motivation for the approach, and having more conclusive experiments.

Nonetheless, I do think that the technical contributions might be there, and I would be happy to raise my score if the authors address the major concerns.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, the authors consider the problem of finding global Nash equilibria in a subclass of non-convex games. The authors claim the following:
  1. They provide a variational inequality problem whose solution corresponds to global Nash equilibria in the class of games that they are interested in.
  2. They construct a continuous time dynamics that converges to a solution of this variational inequality and in particular, it converges exponentially fast with respect to the time parameter of the continuous time dynamics.
  3. They show that in monotone or potential games they can discretize their continuous time dynamics to get an algorithm that converges fast to global Nash Equilibria.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
======================
  - I agree with the general motivation of trying to find subclasses of continuous games for which we can efficiently compute Nash equilibria and hence escape the known hardness results.

Weaknesses - Comments
========================

  1. The main issue with the paper is the writing. The authors skip many important details and even definitions and they refer constantly to the book of Gao, Latorre, and Ruan on Canonical Duality Theory. It seems to me that this paper refers to people from the game theory community as well and if this is the case I believe is to difficult for the reader to assume a good knowledge of the material of this book. At the very least, all the definitions should be restated in the paper.

  2. Another issue with the writing is that they authors never specify what is the class of games that they consider. I think this should be clearly pointed out in a definition environment. Right now, there are some properties that are discussed in the beginning of page 3 but then some other assumptions appear in Section 4 as well and it is not very clear what is the precise set of games that the authors consider.

  Below I assume that the class of games that the authors consider is described in the paragraph in the beginning of page 3.

  3. If the function $J_i$ is not convex with respect to $x_i$ then it is not even clear that a Nash equilibrium exists. How is it possible to design convergent algorithms in setting where equilibrium does not exists? Is there any proof that for these particular functions $J_i$ a Nash equilibrium exists?

  4. The class of games considered is not as limited as it looks and in fact it does not escape the hardness results that we know. Let's assume for simplicity that the domain of all the variables is [0, 1]. Consider now any twice differentiable map $F : [0, 1]^{Nn} \to [0, 1]^{Nn}$. If I understand the assumptions correctly, it is valid to set  
  $J_1(x_1, x_2) = ||x_1 - F(x_2)||^4 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~( \text{where we use }~ \Psi_1(\xi) = \xi^2, \Lambda_1 = \|x_1 - F(x_2)\|^2))$ and  
  $J_2(x_1, x_2) = ||x_1 - x_2||^4 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~( \text{where we use }~ \Psi_2(\xi) = \xi^2, \Lambda_2 = \|x_1 - x_2\|^2)).$  
  It is also easy to observe that the global Nash equilibria, in fact even all the Nash stationary points, are fixed points of the continuous map F. Finding fixed points of continuous maps is a computational problem that is called Brouwer and it is well know that it is PPAD-complete. The only additional assumption here is that F is twice differentiable but there are recent results that show that the problem is PPAD-complete even if F is twice differentiable.
  Additionally, finding fixed points of general maps F is equivalent to solving an appropriate variational inequality. So in fact, finding Nash equilibria in this class of games is as hard as solving all variational inequalities. So, I don't see what the computational advantage of considering this class of games is.

  5. Having convergence results even in the continuous time for this class of games is very surprising. But the actual results are not as strong as we should expect. The statement of Theorem 1 is very weird. Essentially it says that there is a reduction to a VI problem such that *some* solutions of the resulting VI problem correspond to solutions of the original problem. Obviously, there is no way to target these kind of solutions because we do not even know that the original problem has a solution. The same is true for all the results in Section 4. So, it is unclear to me what the theoretical contributions of these results are.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given previous comment, the main contribution of this paper is that it provides a heuristic for solving a very general class of games that includes all fixed point problems. I cannot see any quantitative advantage of the proposed method as it is not even guaranteed to converge to an equilibrium. I believe that at least a more rich experimental section is required to argue for acceptance of this paper.

content.title: Authors' Response
content.comment:
We thank the AC and all reviewers for their precious professional suggestions to enhance the paper's quality.

We are pleased that all reviewers gave positive reviews on the interesting topic and relevant motivation within this paper. Also, they presented satisfaction and recognition concerning the techniques, the theoretical results, and the experiments therein.

Nevertheless, according to the comments, it is a pity that most reviews thought that the way of our writing brought barriers to comprehension and understanding, such as the canonical theory, the applied background of the model, and the technical assumptions. In fact, we had described these points throughout the main body. This kind of deficiency in the Introduction section may probably seem unusual compared to the general styles of ICLR papers, which eventually led to the reviewers’ misgiving. The above fact makes it tough for readers to follow our route, including ignoring the existence conclusion of equilibrium points, confusing about the different assumed conditions, etc.

We thank again for the reviewers’ efforts. The limited time of the rebuttal stage is not enough for us to rearrange the narrative framework of this work, nor to provide a new version with major changes. Thus, we decide to withdraw the article in the hope of polishing the work in the future to make it easier for readers’ comprehension on such an important topic.
